title: The system: play counts and artist royalties for a music service
caption: A streaming path keeps artist dashboards minutes-fresh; a nightly recompute from the raw archive makes the numbers final, and only final numbers are paid out.

steps.text: Players buffer play events (play id, track, start time, seconds listened, country) and upload them in batches. A phone that was offline uploads when it is back.
The ingest API checks each batch and appends it to the play stream, partitioned by track id. A sink copies every event to the raw archive.
The stream processor counts a play only once it reached 30 seconds, drops repeats by play id, and adds it to the event-time minute window for its track and country.
When a window closes it upserts the minute row, and the hour, day and per-artist rows are rolled up from those.
An artist opens the dashboard: the query router reads the coarsest tier that answers the range, a few hundred rows at most.

Each night recon recomputes yesterday from the raw archive, late plays included, overwrites the day rows and marks them final. The monthly statement is built only from final rows and written to the ledger.

scenarios.name: Album release night
scenarios.summary: A big artist releases an album at midnight. A few tracks take a large share of all plays and their partitions run hot.

steps.text: Plays of a dozen new tracks jump to a large share of all traffic within minutes.
Partitioning by track puts each hot track on one processor task, and those tasks start to lag.
Split the hot keys: spread each hot track over several sub-keys, count partial sums in parallel, and add them in a second small stage.
The dashboard shows "data as of" while it catches up. Royalties are not affected: they come from the raw archive.

scenarios.name: Processor crash
scenarios.summary: A processor task dies. It resumes from its last checkpoint, replays the stream, and absolute upserts keep the counts exact.

steps.text: A processor task crashes with several open windows in memory.
A new task loads the last checkpoint (window state, dedup set and stream offsets) and reads the stream again from those offsets.
Rows it writes again are full values, not increments, so writing a minute row twice leaves the same number.
Dashboards were a few minutes stale. The raw archive kept every event, so the nightly numbers are unchanged.

scenarios.name: Dedup bug backfill
scenarios.summary: A release broke dedup and some plays were counted twice for three days. Fix the code, then recompute those days from raw.

steps.text: A diff alert fires: streaming and recon numbers disagree for three days. The cause is a bug in the play-id dedup.
Deploy the fix, then run recon over those three days of raw events.
Recon overwrites the day rows with corrected full values; dashboards change for those days.
The month is still open, so the statement uses the fixed numbers. Had it been issued, the difference would go on next month's statement as an adjustment line.
